title: ‘Slo Pitch’ is swinging to end the one-season queer TV curse | Xtra Magazine
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
‘Slo Pitch’ is swinging to end the one-season queer TV curse | Xtra Magazine

Director J Stevens says the series brings “queer stupidity”—and joy—to our screens

Actual Article Body:

Director J Stevens says the series brings “queer stupidity”—and joy—to our screens

Jess Salgueiro (who plays Coach Joanne Pico) speaks with director J Stevens on the set of “Slo Pitch.”  Credit: Anthony Fascione

Canadian director J Stevens spent their early 20s playing the “weird niche sport” of Australian rules football.

They were the only queer person on the team for their first year, but by year three, “basically everyone on the team was out, everyone was dating everyone and then everyone was breaking up,” they tell me in an interview over Zoom.

The ensuing drama left them with one thought: “this needs to be a TV show.”

Working alongside fellow Canadian showrunners Karen Knox and Gwenlyn Cumyn, Stevens drew from their own queer sports league experience to create Slo Pitch, a new Crave original series produced by Shaftesbury and Elliot Page’s PAGEBOY Productions. The first two episodes are streaming now, with new episodes dropping every Friday.

The show is landing at a time when queer TV is in a weird place. Like many other queer folks out there, I will watch virtually anything that centres queer stories, but these days, those stories are starting to feel few and far between.

Beloved series like Heartstopper, Euphoria and Hacks have wrapped, Yellowjackets is on its last season and even reality shows like I Kissed a Girl and I Kissed a Boy have been getting the chop. When we do get an exciting new series, it’s hard to get attached: so many queer shows—especially ones focusing on women and gender-diverse characters, including Amazon Prime’s 2022 Sapphic baseball show A League of Their Own (RIP)—are cancelled after just one season. Beyond the sudden success of Heated Rivalry, the future of queer TV feels a little uncertain.

But Stevens hopes to offer something new to Sapphic viewers and break the one-season curse with Slo Pitch.

“We love seeing beautiful gay men make out onscreen, but there are others who deserve to see themselves as well,” Stevens says.

Slo Pitch follows the Brovaries, a beer-league softball team in pursuit of their first championship win after their coach’s longtime girlfriend dumps her and joins another team. The mockumentary-style sitcom draws on shows like The Office and Parks and Recreation with its charming (and weird) cast of characters, will-they-won’t-they relationship dynamics and goofy hijinks.

The show began as an OUTtvGo web series in 2020, where it was popular enough to win a second season and be picked up for distribution in the U.S. Now Canadian streamer Crave has rebooted the story as a half-hour comedy, with much of the same cast and creative team.

Stevens describes the resulting show as “queer joy and queer stupidity.” It’s easy to see why, with storylines like the team trying to seduce their coach into ending a team “non-fraternization agreement” and staging a sexy car wash to raise money to pay their league fees.

Despite clear stylistic differences, comparisons between Slo Pitch and Heated Rivalry have been everywhere online. Both shows feature queer characters, revolve around a sport and are Crave original series. But according to Stevens, the similarities stop there. “If you’re coming to our show for Heated Rivalry, you’re going to be sorely disappointed,” they say.
